title: "Design Lab: Drive-Style File Synchronization"
---

# Design Lab: Drive-Style File Synchronization

Build a Go sync service and CLI that move file versions between two local client directories. The goal is correct recovery from offline edits and interrupted uploads. Start with files and folders owned by one account; sharing is a later authorization milestone.

## Separate namespace from content

Give every file a stable file ID, parent ID, display name, current version, and deletion state. Renaming changes metadata; it does not create a new content identity. Store immutable content manifests mapping chunk numbers to blob hashes in the [object-storage lab](05-object-storage.qmd).

Use `POST /uploads`, chunk PUTs, and `POST /files/{id}/commit` carrying the expected base version. Commit verifies all referenced chunks exist, creates one immutable version, and atomically updates the current pointer if the base matches. A mismatched base returns a conflict that clients must resolve explicitly.

In Go, keep the commit operation behind one domain boundary:

```go
type Commit struct {
	FileID, BaseVersion, RequestID string
	Chunks                         []string
}

type FileStore interface {
	Commit(context.Context, Commit) (string, error) // new immutable version
}
```

The implementation must transact namespace update, idempotency result, and change-log insertion together. A hash of content identifies bytes; it does not authorize access to another user's copy. Scope deduplication and chunk fetches to an explicit security model.

## Sync protocol

Provide `GET /changes?cursor=...` as an ordered durable change log. The Go client downloads a page, applies it to its local state, and persists its cursor only after successful application. Write downloaded content to a temporary file and rename after validation. Reject unsafe path components and symlink escapes when mapping remote names locally.

Filesystem watching is an optimization: startup scans and periodic reconciliation recover dropped events. Ignore the client's own temporary files. Use a local pending-operations journal to resume after process exit.

When both clients edit version 7 offline, accept one version-8 commit and reject the other's stale base. Preserve the second edit as a conflict copy rather than silently applying last-writer-wins. Tombstones prevent a returning offline client from resurrecting deleted files. Expired change cursors require a full rescan protocol.

## Acceptance evidence

Disconnect one client, edit on both, reconnect, and inspect both preserved versions. Interrupt every upload stage, repeat commit with the same request ID, and restart after applying a change but before saving its cursor. Verify idempotent replay. Test rename versus edit, delete versus offline edit, and chunk garbage collection while a version is still referenced.

Measure convergence time, missing-chunk retries, bytes deduplicated, and oldest unsynced operation. The pass condition is no silent data loss under the declared conflict and retention policies.
